newsitem.title: SPAIN: CYCLING-INDURAIN RETIRES FROM PROFESSIONAL CYCLING.
newsitem.headline: CYCLING-INDURAIN RETIRES FROM PROFESSIONAL CYCLING.

text.p: Five-times Tour de France winner Miguel Indurain announced his retirement from professional cycling on Thursday.
"I'm going to retire from professional cycling," the 32-year-old Spanish cyclist told journalists at a packed news conference in his home town of Pamplona.
Indurain, who failed to win a sixth consecutive Tour last year and who had to pull out of the Spanish Vuelta, had been debating for some time whether to continue with the sport.
His contract with the Banesto team expired at the end of 1996.

"In the early months of this season I started to turn over the idea that the time had come to give it up and to dedicate myself to the other facets of my life," Indurain said at the news conference, which was broadcast live on Spanish radio.
The decision to retire will be a disappointment to Indurain's Spanish fans who revere him.
"I believe that I have dedicated sufficient time to competitive cycling and now I want to enjoy this sport as an amateur," he said.
Radio announcers said Indurain looked relaxed and was smiling as he spoke.

But Indurain acknowledged that the decision had been tough to make and that many people close to him had encouraged him to try for a record-breaking sixth Tour victory after he pulled out during last year's race.

Indurain, who won the time trial gold medal at last year's Atlanta Olympics, equalled the overall record of five Tour wins set by Jacques Anquetil, Eddy Merckx and Bernard Hinault and was the first rider to collect his five wins in consecutive tours.
"The decision has been tremendously difficult for me because physically I am in good shape and I think I might still be fit enough to win the much-desired sixth Tour," he said.
"I tried to win the Tour with all my strength and I did not succeed. But I won the gold medal in Atlanta. It seemed the perfect close to my sporting career," he added.
